title: Move cookies from a cookie sheet to a cooling rack with a turner, without touching or dropping them
instruction: Move the three cookies from the cookie sheet onto the cooling rack with the turner, in one layer, without touching or dropping them, then put the turner back on its rest.
context: Moving baked cookies from the sheet to a wire rack with a thin metal spatula is a familiar last step of home cookie baking; an oats brand's baking guide says to remove them with a metal spatula, also called a pancake turner, and to 'Cool in single layer on wire cooling rack.' The skill is getting a thin blade under a flat, fragile item, carrying it level and sliding it off onto wires, item after item, with no hand on the food. Non-perishable printed stand-ins replace the cookies so every trial resets the same way.
setup: Positions from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left (arms at y +0.305 and -0.305 m), heights over the table top. (1) Rimless aluminium cookie sheet, 260 x 320 x 1.5 mm, about 0.34 kg, loose, centre at x 0.350, y -0.030, its 320 mm side along y; on it a silicone baking mat, 240 x 300 x 0.75 mm. (2) Three cookie stand-ins: printed PLA discs at an oatmeal cookie's size and weight (USDA FoodData Central lists one oatmeal cookie, prepared from recipe, at 2-5/8 in across and 15 g), 66.7 mm across, 6 mm thick, 15 g (infill set to that weight), tan, the underside edge eased (the flat bottom ends 4 mm inside the rim and the edge rises 1.5 mm), lying flat on the mat with centres at x 0.360 and y +0.050, -0.040, -0.130. (3) Wire cooling rack, loose, 200 x 360 mm (360 along y), wire tops 20 mm over the table, 2 mm wires every 12 mm running along y on a 4 mm frame and four feet, about 0.25 kg, centre at x 0.320, y -0.380. (4) Stainless offset turner (cookie spatula), 73 g: blade 90 mm long and 86 mm wide (wider than a cookie), 1.0 mm thick at the neck ground to 0.3 mm at the tip edge, its underside 35 mm below a 100 x 22 x 14 mm soft-grip handle; it lies on its rest with the blade flat on the table pointing away from the robot (+x) and the handle's middle (50 mm from either end of the handle) at x 0.070, y -0.600; the handle's front end, where the neck starts, is then at x 0.120. (5) The rest: a wood block 30 x 30 x 28 mm fixed to the table with double-sided tape under the back of the handle, centre at x 0.040, y -0.600 (the handle's back end overhangs it by 5 mm). Both arms start in the ready pose.
scoring: Each cookie that was carried on the turner's blade (at some step its centre over the blade and its underside within 3 mm of the blade's top, 10 mm or more over the mat), then ends off the blade lying flat (within 10 degrees) on the rack's wires, in one layer (its underside within 3 mm of the wire tops, not on another cookie), with its whole outline over the rack's outline (2 mm grace), at rest, never touched by the robot (any point of either arm's links every link but the base and link 1, to the finger tips within 3 mm counts in simulation; any contact seen on the video in a real trial) and never dropped (falling faster than 0.6 m/s, or 18 mm lower than 0.1 s before), scores 0.25. A touched or dropped cookie never counts, wherever it ends. Score 1.0 when all three count and, held for 1 second, the turner lies back on its rest (the handle's middle within 20 mm of x 0.070, y -0.600, pointing within 15 degrees, resting on the rest), the sheet and the rack are each within 30 mm of their starting places, the sheet was never tilted over 5 degrees nor raised 5 mm at any step (so tipping the cookies off with the other arm gets no full score), nothing moves, every gripper point is at least 30 mm from each cookie and from the turner, and both arms were read at every step. Otherwise the score is 0.25 per counted cookie (at most 0.75). Doing nothing scores 0. Real trial: a photo from above for the rack outline, a ruler or side photo for flat and single layer and for the sheet staying flat, a ruler against tape marks for the turner, sheet and rack, and the video for touches, drops and the carry on the blade.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed or worn. Set the three stand-ins flat on the mat on their marks (eased edge down), the sheet and rack on their tape outlines, and the turner on its rest. Before each session, wipe the mat, blade and stand-ins clean and repeat the tilt test in the README.
fidelity: True-size rigid bodies in PhysX with real contact; the 1 mm tapered blade is a collider and gets under each stand-in through its eased edge. Friction is fixed: PLA on the mat 0.75, on steel 0.25. The stand-ins are rigid and cannot break, so touches and drops, which spoil a real cookie, are scored instead; the blade is wider than the cookie, so a cookie centred on it does not overhang it. Touches are a distance from the arm's link collision models, not a contact force.
